title: Katakana H-Row — ハ ヒ フ ヘ ホ

points.name: ハ
points.explanation: ハ makes the same 'ha' sound as hiragana は. Visually, ハ looks like two diagonal strokes leaning apart from each other, like a pair of legs standing wide — or like the Roman letter 'A' without the crossbar. This simple two-stroke character is quite easy to write and remember. ハ appears in ハンバーガー (hamburger), ハーモニー (harmony), and ハンド (hand). In Japanese cultural contexts, ハーフ (half, meaning a person of mixed heritage) and ハイ (hai, the Japanese word for 'yes' written in katakana for emphasis) are also commonly seen.
rules: Same 'ha' as は — breathy 'h' + open 'ah' vowel.
ハ = two strokes spreading apart. Looks like an 'A' without the crossbar.
Memory: ハ looks like two legs standing wide, making an open 'ha!' sound.
points.flashcardAnswer: ha — same sound as は; looks like two legs standing wide

points.name: ヒ
points.explanation: ヒ makes the same 'hi' sound as hiragana ひ. Visually, ヒ looks like a capital letter 'F' or 'E' with only two arms — a vertical stroke on the left and two horizontal strokes extending to the right, with the lower horizontal being shorter. Some describe ヒ as looking like a backward 'F'. Compare this to hiragana ひ, which has a flowing cursive structure. ヒ appears in ヒーロー (hero), ヒント (hint), and ヒット (hit — as in a hit song or hit product). The elongation in ヒーロー makes the first 'i' two beats long.
rules: Same 'hi' as ひ — slightly palatal 'h' + bright 'ee' vowel.
ヒ looks like a backwards 'F' — vertical stroke on the left, two horizontals extending right.
ヒント (hint) is commonly used in Japanese conversation and games.
points.flashcardAnswer: hi — same sound as ひ; looks like a backwards 'F'

points.name: フ
points.shortDescription: Same sound as ふ — the unique bilabial 'fu'
points.explanation: フ makes the same unique bilabial 'fu' sound as hiragana ふ — lips come close together but don't fully stop the air, creating a sound between 'f' and 'h'. Visually, フ is wonderfully simple: just two strokes forming a shape like a hook or a reversed comma on a shelf — a horizontal stroke with a diagonal curl downward on the right end. Some see it as resembling a simplified fishhook or the Roman letter 'J' on a shelf. フ appears in フランス (France), フルーツ (fruit), フォーク (fork), and フリー (free).
rules: Same bilabial 'fu' as ふ — both lips close, not teeth-and-lip like English 'f'.
フ = horizontal stroke + curling diagonal. Looks like a hook or reversed 'J' on a shelf.
フ begins many French-origin loanwords: フランス (France), フロマージュ (cheese from French).
points.flashcardAnswer: fu — same bilabial sound as ふ; looks like a hook or reversed 'J'

points.name: ヘ
points.shortDescription: Same sound as へ — 'he' (or 'e' as particle)
points.explanation: ヘ makes the same 'he' sound as hiragana へ. This is a remarkable case where the hiragana and katakana characters look almost identical — both are a simple mountain-peak shape (a V with the point at the top). Hiragana へ curves slightly; katakana ヘ tends to be more angular, but they're the closest pair in the entire kana system. ヘ appears in ヘルメット (helmet), ヘアドライヤー (hair dryer), and ヘルス (health). Because hiragana and katakana へ look so similar, you can easily recognize ヘ if you already know へ.
rules: Same 'he' as へ — or 'e' (no 'h') when used as the directional particle.
ヘ and へ look nearly identical — a mountain-peak shape. Katakana is slightly more angular.
This is the closest hiragana-katakana pair in the entire system.
points.flashcardAnswer: he — same sound as へ; looks almost identical to hiragana へ

points.name: ホ
points.explanation: ホ makes the same 'ho' sound as hiragana ほ. Visually, ホ looks like a cross or plus-sign with an extra diagonal stroke extending from the lower-right area — some describe it as a telephone pole with a lean. It has four strokes and is more complex than other H-row characters. Compare this to hiragana ほ, which has a completely different flowing structure. ホ appears in ホテル (hotel), ホーム (platform / home), and ホワイト (white). ホテルはどこですか? (Where is the hotel?) is essential travel vocabulary.
rules: ホ looks like a cross/plus with an added diagonal — four strokes, more complex than other H-row katakana.
ホテル (hotel) is survival vocabulary for any traveler to Japan.
points.flashcardAnswer: ho — same sound as ほ; looks like a cross with an added diagonal

chapterPractice.prompt: ヘ and へ look almost identical. What sound do they both make?
chapterPractice.explanation: ヘ makes the 'he' sound — same as hiragana へ. These two characters are the most visually similar hiragana-katakana pair in the entire system. Both look like a mountain peak or angled roof shape.

chapterPractice.prompt: Which hiragana matches the katakana ハ?
chapterPractice.explanation: ハ and は both make the 'ha' sound. Katakana ハ looks like two legs spread wide (an 'A' without the crossbar), while hiragana は has a more complex, flowing four-stroke structure.

chapterPractice.prompt: What does this katakana word mean?
chapterPractice.explanation: ホテル (hoteru) means 'hotel'. ホ (ho) + テ (te) + ル (ru) = hoteru. Essential travel vocabulary — you'll need to find one on your first trip to Japan!

chapterPractice.prompt: What does this katakana word mean?
chapterPractice.explanation: ヒント (hinto) means 'hint'. ヒ (hi) + ン (n) + ト (to) = hinto. This word is used constantly in Japanese games, quizzes, and everyday conversation.
